chunks: How and when PCBs are tested. The question: How are PCBs tested? When does this happen?
Boards are tested at several points on their way to becoming a product, and each test catches a different kind of problem. The bare board is checked for broken or shorted copper.
Cameras check the soldering. Electrical tests check that the right parts are present and connected. A final test checks that the board does its job.
The goal is to catch each defect as early and cheaply as possible.
Think of a bakery. The baker checks the flour before mixing, looks at the dough before baking, and checks the loaf when it comes out. Only at the end does someone taste it.
If the flour was bad, you want to know before baking, not after. A board line works the same way.
The final taste test is slow and does not tell you why something is wrong, so it comes last.
Each gate is cheaper per board and more specific early in the line, and broader but slower later.
Which gates a product uses depends on volume, cost of failure and board complexity.
Bare-board test: an electrical check at the board factory for opens (broken connections) and shorts (unwanted connections) in the copper.
AOI: automated optical inspection, a camera check of the soldering and parts. In-circuit test: probes touch the board to check for shorts, opens and part values.
Functional test: powering the board and checking that it behaves like the real product. First-pass yield: the fraction of boards that pass a stage with no repair.
Say AOI passes 99 % of boards at first try, in-circuit test passes 97 %, and functional test passes 95 %. A board must pass all three, so the overall first-pass yield is 0.
99 x 0. 97 x 0. 95 = about 91. 2 %. A defect found by AOI costs a quick fix. The same defect found at functional test costs far more diagnosis time.
A rough rule of thumb says the cost grows about tenfold per stage. That is the whole idea.
"Boards are tested in layers. The fab tests bare boards for opens and shorts. In assembly, SPI and AOI check paste and placement and X-ray checks hidden joints.
After assembly, in-circuit or flying probe test finds opens, shorts and wrong or missing components, and functional test powers the board and checks it works.
Some products get burn-in or thermal cycling too. The idea is to catch defects as early as possible since each later stage costs more to diagnose and fix."
